children.value: Learning Goals
By the end of this tutorial, you will:
Understand the basic characteristics of Euclid DR1 MER catalogs.
Know which of the four DR1 MER catalog tables to use.
What columns are available in the MER catalog.
How to search the MER catalog around a position on the sky.
How to use the MER quality columns to clean a catalog.
How to select stars and compute their total fluxes in the Euclid and ground-based bands.
How to look at the MER VIS images of catalog sources.
How to query the MER catalog with ADQL and make a color-color diagram of stars.
Introduction

Euclid launched in July 2023 as a European Space Agency (ESA) mission with involvement by NASA.
The primary science goals of Euclid are to better understand the composition and evolution of the dark Universe.
The Euclid mission is providing space-based imaging and spectroscopy as well as supporting ground-based imaging to achieve these primary goals.
These data are archived by multiple global repositories, including IRSA, where they will support transformational work in many areas of astrophysics.

Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) comprises about 1900 sq deg of imaging, spectroscopy, and catalogs from the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), which will eventually cover about 14,000 sq deg, and from the Euclid Deep Survey (EDS), which covers about 53 sq deg in the three Euclid Deep Fields (North, South, and Fornax).
DR1 also includes several photometric redshift and instrument calibration fields, such as COSMOS, CDFS, and AEGIS.
It follows Quick Release 1 (Q1), which covered about 63 sq deg with a single pass over each of the three Euclid Deep Fields and the dark cloud LDN 1641; all of the DR1 data, including the areas observed in Q1, have been reprocessed with updated pipelines and calibrations.

Among the data products included in DR1 are the MER catalogs.
MER (the Merge processing function of the Euclid ground segment) combines the VIS, NISP, and ground-based images into mosaics on a common grid, and detects and measures the sources on them to build the MER catalog.
The MER processing detects sources on the VIS and NISP mosaics (see the
MER mosaics notebook

) and measures their photometry in the Euclid VIS, Y, J, H bands and in the accompanying ground-based u, g, r, i, z bands, along with other basic measurements, like size and shape.
This notebook provides an introduction to the MER final catalog, in which each entry is a single source.
In this notebook we follow a typical path through the MER catalog: we search for the sources around a position on the sky, clean the sample with the quality columns, select the stars, look at the spectral energy distributions and VIS images of a few of them, and finally make a color-color diagram of many stars.
The MER processing for DR1 is described in detail in Euclid Collaboration: Kümmel et al. (2026), see the
References

section below.
The release as a whole is described in Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. (2026) and the surveys it covers in Euclid Collaboration: Tereno et al. (2026).
If you have questions about this notebook, please contact the
IRSA helpdesk
The MER catalog tables

The DR1 MER catalog is split into four tables, according to how the data were observed and which MER tiling was used, plus two companion photometry tables for the deep tiles.
MER processes the sky in tiles:
wide
tiles (tile IDs starting with
, about 32 x 32 arcmin, the same tiling as in Q1) and smaller
deep
tiles (tile IDs starting with
, about 17 x 17 arcmin), used for fields too deep to process as wide tiles.
euclid_dr1_mer_catalogue_wide_survey
the Euclid Wide Survey
, the standard-depth survey intended for cosmology (wide tiles).
If you are looking for the standard Euclid survey, this is the table you want
, and it is the one used in this notebook.
euclid_dr1_mer_catalogue_deep_survey
the Euclid Deep Survey
: the deep stacks of the Euclid Deep Fields North, South, and Fornax (deep tiles).
euclid_dr1_mer_catalogue_deep_mode
-- other fields deep enough to need the deep tiling, but not part of the Deep Survey: the Euclid auxiliary fields COSMOS, CDFS, and AEGIS.
euclid_dr1_mer_catalogue_wide_mode

-- other fields processed with the wide tiling that are neither part of the Wide Survey nor visits of the deep fields, for example some of the fields observed during the thermal stabilization period of the PSF calibration campaign, just before the main survey started (January/February 2024).
euclid_dr1_mer_catalogue_deep_survey_photometry
and
euclid_dr1_mer_catalogue_deep_mode_photometry

-- companion tables for the deep tiles, with photometry in the additional external bands that are only available in the deep and auxiliary fields (for example Spitzer/IRAC, GALEX, VISTA, and the Subaru intermediate bands). They can be joined to the corresponding main table on
object_id
The
wide_survey
and
wide_mode
sources are measured on the wide-tile mosaics, and the
deep_survey
and
deep_mode

sources on the deep-tile mosaics.
In the deep fields, the wide tiles also have single-pass “deep visit” mosaics (see the
MER mosaics notebook
); the wide-tile catalog in these fields comes from the official wide survey mosaic only.

The deep fields are covered by both the Deep Survey (deep tiles) and the wide tiling, so the same object can appear in more than one table, measured on data of different depth.
Table 5 of Kümmel et al. (2026) lists all of the DR1 fields with their tiling and exposure times.
The MER catalog from the earlier Quick Release 1 (Q1) is also available at IRSA, as the single table
euclid_q1_mer_catalogue

.
All of the Q1 areas have been reprocessed for DR1, so Q1 and DR1 fluxes should not be mixed (see the
notes on the DR1 MER photometry
below).

children.label: 1. Find the MER catalog tables at IRSA

children.value: The DR1 MER catalog is far too large to download, so we use IRSA’s services to run queries on the server and retrieve only the rows and columns we need.
First, have a look at what Euclid catalogs are available. With the

functionality, we’ll receive a list of the name of the catalogs as well as their brief desciption.

children.value: Choose the Euclid MER table

We use the Wide Survey table. You can change the table name here to use one of the other DR1 MER tables described above, but the rest of this notebook assumes a field with DECam ground-based photometry (g, r, i, z), as at our search position; elsewhere, adjust the bands in the following cells to the ground-based bands available there.
The deep tables have many more sources per area, so use a much smaller search radius with them (for example 0.05 deg) and a position in one of the deep fields.
We run the query asynchronously (
async_job=True
), so that larger queries do not time out.
table_mer = 'euclid_dr1_mer_catalogue_wide_survey'

columns_info
Tip
Each DR1 MER catalog table contains 480 columns, below are a few highlights:
object_id

flux_y_templfit, flux_j_templfit, flux_h_templfit: template-fitting fluxes
flux_vis_to_y_templfit, flux_vis_to_j_templfit, flux_vis_to_h_templfit: template-fitting fluxes measured on the VIS image degraded to the resolution of each NIR band
fwhm

2. Search the MER catalog around a position

children.label: 2. Search the MER catalog around a position

children.value:
We start with all of the sources within 0.5 deg of a position in the Wide Survey.
This area contains a few hundred thousand sources, so rather than retrieving all 480 columns, we write an ADQL query that returns only the columns we need for this notebook:
the positions and tile IDs, the quality columns, the star-galaxy classification, and the template-fitting fluxes in the Euclid and ground-based bands (see section 5).
The
CONTAINS
and
CIRCLE
functions select the sources in a circle on the sky.

coord = SkyCoord(ra=90.7299, dec=-45.3529, unit='deg')
search_radius = 0.5 * u.deg

# Template-fitting fluxes in the Euclid NIR bands and in all of the ground-based bands
flux_cols = ([f'flux_{band}_templfit' for band in 'yjh'] + [f'flux_vis_to_{band}_templfit' for band in 'yjh']
             + [col for col in columns_info
                if col.startswith('flux_') and '_ext_' in col and col.endswith('_templfit')])
columns = (['object_id', 'ra', 'dec', 'tileid', 'vis_det', 'flux_detection_total',
            'point_like_flag', 'point_like_prob', 'spurious_prob', 'det_quality_flag',
            'flag_vis', 'flag_y', 'flag_j', 'flag_h'] + flux_cols)

adql = (f"SELECT {', '.join(columns)} "
        f"FROM {table_mer} "
        "WHERE CONTAINS(POINT('ICRS', ra, dec), "
        f"CIRCLE('ICRS', {coord.ra.deg}, {coord.dec.deg}, {search_radius.to_value(u.deg)})) = 1")

# Alternatively, uncomment the query below to get 10,000 stars from anywhere in the table instead of all of the
# sources around a position. The sky map below assumes a search around a position, so skip it in that case.
# adql = f"SELECT TOP 10000 {', '.join(columns)} FROM {table_mer} WHERE point_like_flag = 1"
We run the query with the TAP service, which takes about a minute.

result = Irsa.query_tap(adql, async_job=True).to_table()

# Keep only the sources with a positive total flux in the detection band, so that we can compute magnitudes
result = result[result['flux_detection_total'] > 0]
print(len(result))
Tip
For a small search area, the
query_region
method of
astroquery
is a simpler alternative to writing ADQL, and it can return all of the columns, for example:
Irsa.query_region(coordinates=coord, spatial='Cone', catalog=table_mer, radius=3 * u.arcmin, columns='*')

Let’s look at the density of sources on the sky, as offsets from the center of the search.
The MER catalog is built tile by tile, and the map shows the tile structure, areas without sources (for example around bright stars), and the edge of the DR1 coverage.

source_coords = SkyCoord(ra=result['ra'], dec=result['dec'], unit='deg')
offset_ra, offset_dec = coord.spherical_offsets_to(source_coords)
offset_ra = offset_ra.to_value(u.arcmin)
offset_dec = offset_dec.to_value(u.arcmin)

limit = 1.05 * search_radius.to_value(u.arcmin)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))
_, _, _, image = ax.hist2d(offset_ra, offset_dec, bins=np.linspace(-limit, limit, 120), cmap='Greys')
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label='Number of sources per bin')
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), search_radius.to_value(u.arcmin), fill=False, linestyle='--', color='tab:blue'))
ax.set_xlim(limit, -limit)  # RA increases to the left
ax.set_ylim(-limit, limit)
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.set_xlabel('RA offset (arcmin)')
ax.set_ylabel('Dec offset (arcmin)')
plt.show()
3. Clean the sample with the quality columns

children.label: 3. Clean the sample with the quality columns

children.value: Before using the sources, we check the MER columns that identify sources whose detection or photometry may be unreliable:
spurious_prob
is the probability that a source is a spurious detection, for example an artifact around a bright object.
spurious_flag
is set for
spurious_prob > 0.5
, but this has proven too aggressive, and a threshold of 0.7 is suggested instead (see the
notes on the DR1 MER photometry
below).
flag_vis
flag_y
flag_j
, and
flag_h
keep track of the flagged pixels (for example bad or saturated pixels) in the flag image of each band.
det_quality_flag
flags problems in the detection step that could corrupt the magnitude used for the star-galaxy separation.
Nonzero flags do not necessarily mean that a source is unusable, but they are worth checking for your science case.

is_spurious = result['spurious_prob'] > 0.7
print(f"spurious_prob > 0.5: {np.sum(result['spurious_prob'] > 0.5)} of {len(result)} sources")
print(f"spurious_prob > 0.7: {np.sum(is_spurious)} of {len(result)} sources")
print(f"flag_vis != 0: {np.sum(result['flag_vis'] != 0)} of {len(result)} sources")
print(f"det_quality_flag != 0: {np.sum(result['det_quality_flag'] != 0)} of {len(result)} sources")

clean_sources = result[~is_spurious]

4. Select the stars
The MER catalog does not have a column for classification, but it provides
point_like_prob
, the probability that a VIS-detected source is point-like.
point_like_flag = 1
selects VIS-detected sources with
point_like_prob > 0.96

, the threshold that reached a 99% star purity in simulations.
A lower
point_like_prob
threshold gives a more complete but less pure star sample.

# point_like_flag is only set for VIS-detected sources; masked values count as 0
stars = clean_sources[(np.ma.filled(clean_sources['point_like_flag'], 0) == 1)
                      & (clean_sources['vis_det'] == 1)]
print(len(stars))
5. Look at the SEDs and VIS images of three stars

children.label: 5. Look at the SEDs and VIS images of three stars

children.value: Total fluxes in the Euclid and ground-based bands

children.label: Total fluxes in the Euclid and ground-based bands

children.value:
Besides the Euclid VIS, Y, J, and H bands, the MER catalog contains photometry measured on ground-based images in the u, g, r, i, and z bands.
Which ground-based surveys are available depends on the position on the sky, for example DECam in the south, or a combination of MegaCam, HSC, and Pan-STARRS in the north (Euclid Collaboration: Corcho-Caballero et al. 2026).
The catalog therefore has columns for all of the possible survey and band combinations, named
flux_<band>_ext_<survey>_...

, and only some of them are filled at a given position.
Let’s check which ground-based bands have measurements for our stars.

children.value: At this position, the ground-based photometry comes from DECam, in the g, r, i, and z bands.

To get total fluxes, we follow the recipe of the MER Photometry Cookbook in the Euclid DR1 Data Product Description Document (DPDD).
The total flux of an object is measured with a Kron aperture in the detection band, which is VIS for VIS-detected objects (
vis_det = 1
), and is given in
flux_detection_total

.
The total flux in another band X, from Euclid or from the ground, is then obtained by scaling the detection-band total flux with the color measured by template fitting:
F_{X,\mathrm{tot}} = \mathtt{flux\_detection\_total} \times \frac{\mathtt{flux\_X\_templfit}}{\mathtt{flux\_vis\_to\_X\_templfit}}
children.html: FX,tot=flux_detection_total×flux_X_templfitflux_vis_to_X_templfitF_{X,\mathrm{tot}} = \mathtt{flux\_detection\_total} \times \frac{\mathtt{flux\_X\_templfit}}{\mathtt{flux\_vis\_to\_X\_templfit}}FX,tot​=flux_detection_total×flux_vis_to_X_templfitflux_X_templfit​

children.value: where
flux_vis_to_X_templfit

is the template-fitting flux measured on the VIS image degraded to the resolution of band X.
The cookbook gives an equivalent recipe with the aperture fluxes (
flux_X_nfwhm_aper / flux_vis_nfwhm_aper

).
The fluxes are in uJy, which we convert to AB magnitudes.
Choose three stars

We pick three stars with positive fluxes in all bands, no flagged pixels in the Euclid bands, no detection problems, and of intermediate brightness.
To span the range of stellar colors, we take the stars closest to three points along the stellar locus in the VIS - J vs. J - H color-color diagram that we make below: a blue, an intermediate, and a red star.

# Approximate central wavelengths of the bands, in micron
band_wavelengths = {'g_ext_decam': 0.48, 'r_ext_decam': 0.64, 'vis': 0.72, 'i_ext_decam': 0.78,
                    'z_ext_decam': 0.92, 'y': 1.08, 'j': 1.37, 'h': 1.77}

has_all_bands = has_positive_fluxes(stars, band_wavelengths)
mag_vis = total_mag(stars, 'vis')
no_flags = ((stars['flag_vis'] == 0) & (stars['flag_y'] == 0) & (stars['flag_j'] == 0) & (stars['flag_h'] == 0)
            & (stars['det_quality_flag'] == 0))
candidates = stars[has_all_bands & no_flags & (mag_vis > 18.5) & (mag_vis < 21)]

color_vis_j = total_mag(candidates, 'vis') - total_mag(candidates, 'j')
color_j_h = total_mag(candidates, 'j') - total_mag(candidates, 'h')
# (VIS - J, J - H) of a blue, an intermediate, and a red star on the stellar locus
locus_points = [(0.0, -0.2), (0.5, -0.03), (1.5, 0.03)]
three_stars = candidates[[np.argmin(np.hypot(color_vis_j - x, color_j_h - y)) for x, y in locus_points]]
three_stars['object_id', 'ra', 'dec', 'tileid']
The MER
object_id

is built from the position of the source: its digits are the RA and the absolute value of the Dec, both in units of 1e-7 deg, and its sign is the sign of the Dec.
All of our sources are in the southern sky, so they have negative IDs.
Get VIS cutouts of the three stars

children.label: Get VIS cutouts of the three stars

children.value: The MER mosaics are available through IRSA’s Simple Image Access (SIA) service and are hosted in the cloud (see the
MER mosaics notebook

for more details).
For each star, we search for the VIS mosaics at its position (in the wide or deep collection, depending on its tile), and read a small cutout directly from the cloud, without downloading the full mosaic.
Each source in the MER catalog belongs to one tile, so we use the mosaic of the tile given by its
tileid

def get_s3_fpath(cloud_access):
    cloud_info = json.loads(cloud_access)  # converts str to dict
    return f"{cloud_info['aws']['bucket_name']}/{cloud_info['aws']['key']}"


def vis_cutout(source, size=10 * u.arcsec):
    position = SkyCoord(ra=source['ra'], dec=source['dec'], unit='deg')
    # Deep tile IDs start with 101, wide tile IDs with 102
    if str(source['tileid']).startswith('101'):
        collection = 'euclid_dr1_deep_DpdMerBksMosaic'
    else:
        collection = 'euclid_dr1_wide_DpdMerBksMosaic'
    sia_results = Irsa.query_sia(pos=(position, 1 * u.arcsec), collection=collection)
    # The tile ID is the first part of the obs_id of the mosaic
    is_vis_mosaic = ((sia_results['dataproduct_subtype'] == 'science') & (sia_results['energy_bandpassname'] == 'VIS')
                     & [obs_id.startswith(str(source['tileid'])) for obs_id in sia_results['obs_id']])
    mosaic = sia_results[is_vis_mosaic][0]
    with fits.open(f"s3://{get_s3_fpath(mosaic['cloud_access'])}", fsspec_kwargs={'anon': True}) as hdu:
        return Cutout2D(hdu[0].section, position=position, size=size, wcs=WCS(hdu[0].header)).data


cutouts = [vis_cutout(star) for star in three_stars]
Plot the SEDs and the images

children.label: Plot the SEDs and the images

children.value:
star_colors = ['tab:blue', 'tab:green', 'tab:red']

# The SEDs on the left, and the three VIS cutouts stacked in a narrow column on the right
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
grid = fig.add_gridspec(3, 2, width_ratios=[4, 1])
ax_sed = fig.add_subplot(grid[:, 0])
for star, color in zip(three_stars, star_colors):
    mags = [total_mag(star, band) for band in band_wavelengths]
    ax_sed.plot(list(band_wavelengths.values()), mags, 'o-', color=color, label=f"object_id {star['object_id']}")
ax_sed.invert_yaxis()
ax_sed.set_xscale('log')
ax_sed.set_xticks(list(band_wavelengths.values()), ['g', 'r', 'VIS', 'i', 'z', 'Y', 'J', 'H'])
ax_sed.minorticks_off()
ax_sed.set_xlabel('Band (approximate central wavelength on a log scale)')
ax_sed.set_ylabel('Total AB magnitude')
ax_sed.legend()

for i, (star, cutout, color) in enumerate(zip(three_stars, cutouts, star_colors)):
    ax = fig.add_subplot(grid[i, 1])
    norm = ImageNormalize(cutout, interval=PercentileInterval(99.9), stretch=AsinhStretch())
    ax.imshow(cutout, origin='lower', cmap='gray', norm=norm)
    ax.set_title(f"VIS = {total_mag(star, 'vis'):.1f}", color=color, fontsize='medium')
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    for spine in ax.spines.values():
        spine.set_edgecolor(color)
        spine.set_linewidth(3)
fig.tight_layout()

All three stars are point sources in the VIS images, but their SEDs have very different shapes.
The bluest star is hot, with a nearly flat SED in AB magnitudes, while the cooler stars are much fainter in the blue bands than in the near-infrared.
A color-color diagram captures these differences for many stars at once.
6. Make a color-color diagram of the stars

children.label: 6. Make a color-color diagram of the stars

children.value:
Finally, we make a color-color diagram of all of the stars in our search area.
Some sources have no measurement in a band, for example where a tile is only partially covered (see the
notes on the DR1 MER photometry

below).
These fluxes are masked in the table, and faint sources can also have negative fluxes, so we keep only the stars with positive fluxes in all of the bands we need.

cc_bands = ['j', 'h', 'g_ext_decam', 'r_ext_decam']
has_all_fluxes = has_positive_fluxes(stars, cc_bands)
many_stars = stars[has_all_fluxes]
print(f"{len(many_stars)} of {len(stars)} stars have VIS, J, H, g, and r fluxes")

color_x = total_mag(many_stars, 'vis') - total_mag(many_stars, 'j')
color_y = total_mag(many_stars, 'j') - total_mag(many_stars, 'h')
color_g_r = total_mag(many_stars, 'g_ext_decam') - total_mag(many_stars, 'r_ext_decam')

children.value: We plot the stars as points colored by their ground-based g - r color, add contours of the density of stars, and mark the three stars from above.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))
image = ax.scatter(color_x, color_y, c=color_g_r, s=5, alpha=0.6, cmap='coolwarm', vmin=0, vmax=1.6, edgecolor='none')
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label='g - r (DECam)')

# Contours of the star counts in coarser bins, which smooths them
counts, xedges, yedges = np.histogram2d(color_x, color_y,
                                        bins=[np.arange(-0.75, 2.6, 0.12), np.arange(-0.6, 0.65, 0.05)])
ax.contour((xedges[:-1] + xedges[1:]) / 2, (yedges[:-1] + yedges[1:]) / 2, counts.T,
           levels=[5, 15, 40], colors='black', linewidths=0.8)

for star, color in zip(three_stars, star_colors):
    ax.scatter(total_mag(star, 'vis') - total_mag(star, 'j'), total_mag(star, 'j') - total_mag(star, 'h'),
               s=250, marker='*', color=color, edgecolor='black', linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)

ax.set_xlim(-0.75, 2.5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 0.6)
ax.set_xlabel('VIS - J')
ax.set_ylabel('J - H')
ax.set_title(f'{len(many_stars)} stars in the DR1 MER Wide Survey catalog -- IRSA')
plt.show()

The stars follow the stellar locus, a narrow sequence in color-color space set mainly by their temperature.
From hot to cool stars, both colors first become redder together, then J - H stays nearly constant while VIS - J keeps increasing: for the coolest stars, the M dwarfs, molecular absorption shapes the near-infrared spectrum and J - H no longer tracks temperature.
The longer wavelength baseline of VIS - J keeps separating these stars, and our three stars lie at different positions along the locus.
The ground-based g - r color, which also traces temperature, changes smoothly along the locus, from the blue, hot stars to the red, cool ones.
Notes on the DR1 MER photometry

children.label: Notes on the DR1 MER photometry

children.value:
Kümmel et al. (2026) describe the DR1 MER photometry and its known limitations in detail, and Euclid Collaboration: Gasparetto et al. (2026) validate the multi-band photometry on extragalactic sources in the COSMOS field.
The processing and calibration of the NISP images are described in Euclid Collaboration: Polenta et al. (2026), and the photometric masks of DR1 in Euclid Collaboration: Odier et al. (2026).
The most important points for using the catalog are:
NIR calibration offsets

: the Euclid Y, J, and H fluxes have offsets of a few to about 13 percent with respect to Gaia, depending on the photometric method. The offsets are similar in the three bands, so NIR colors are more reliable than absolute NIR magnitudes.
Partial coverage

: some tiles are only partially covered, at the survey borders or in individual bands, for example after solar proton events. Requiring a detection in all bands therefore removes sources in these areas.
Spurious sources
spurious_flag
is set for
spurious_prob > 0.5
, which has proven too aggressive; a threshold of 0.7 is suggested instead. The spurious probability is optimized for wide data.
Note

If you have used the Euclid Quick Release 1 (Q1) MER catalog: the DR1 PSFs are no longer normalized to unit flux.
This corrects the large offsets seen in Q1 for bands with extended PSFs (such as Pan-STARRS i), but means that DR1 fluxes differ systematically from the Q1 ones, so the two releases should not be mixed.
Colors measured with aperture (A-PHOT) or template-fitting (T-PHOT) photometry are largely unaffected.

In The Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) is an initiative of ESA and the Euclid Consortium. The core content of Euclid DR1 includes wide survey observations for a total sky coverage of about 1900 deg2. Roughly 500 deg2 are observations taken in the Northern hemisphere and 1400 deg2 are taken in the Southern hemisphere. In addition to the wide survey: Vol. DR1 also includes data from the Euclid deep fields (p. as well as observations taken before the start of the nominal survey.).
